title: React Teacher Administration & Reporting Dashboard
description: I designed and built the 2019 React replacement for the Essential Skills Teacher Dashboard, rebuilding the earlier JavaScript administration and reporting system as a production React application. I handled the UI/UX redesign, frontend architecture, request orchestration, reporting, teacher/admin workflows, and integration with the existing PHP, AWS, and SimpleDB backend. The React generation became the long-term production Teacher Dashboard and was never replaced.

sections.title: 2019 React Replacement
paragraphs: This application replaced the earlier JavaScript-based Teacher Dashboard in 2019.
I rebuilt the administration and reporting experience in React while preserving and extending the platform capabilities that schools already depended on.

sections.title: Solo Development
paragraphs: I built the React Teacher Dashboard myself.
I designed the UI/UX and then reviewed the resulting direction with the company owners for approval.

sections.title: Production Full-Stack Architecture
paragraphs: React formed the frontend while the existing production backend remained primarily PHP, AWS, and SimpleDB.
The application used Axios, Redux, Redux-Observable, and RxJS to coordinate communication between the browser and backend services.

sections.title: Centralized Request Pipeline
paragraphs: The conventional Redux / Redux-Observable approach created excessive boilerplate for the number of backend operations in the dashboard.
A straightforward endpoint could require roughly seven related files, which did not scale well as the application grew.
I replaced the repeated per-endpoint structure with a centralized request pipeline that routed all requests through one shared set of Redux/RxJS infrastructure.

sections.title: Declarative Request Descriptors
paragraphs: Feature code created request descriptors containing the backend function name and parameters rather than creating a new Redux/RxJS implementation for every operation.
The shared request system interpreted those descriptors, sent the request to the backend, and returned the results through the common state-management path.

sections.title: Chained Request Orchestration
paragraphs: The request model supported a nextRequest property that allowed one completed request to trigger the next request in a sequence.
This made multi-step initialization and data-loading flows declarative without scattering orchestration across many components or duplicating transport infrastructure.

sections.title: Teacher and Administrator Access
paragraphs: The dashboard supported both teacher and administrator accounts.
Teachers worked within their own classes and students, while school administrators could access and manage all teachers within the school.

sections.title: Class and Student Management
paragraphs: The React generation handled the core teacher-management workflows for classes and students.
This was also the generation where students could belong to multiple classes even when the school was not using an external rostering integration.
items: Group students for assignments and reports

sections.title: Assignments and Assessment Workflows
paragraphs: Teachers could assign complete programs or selected sections to individual students, groups, or classes.
The dashboard also integrated the suite's pretest and posttest workflows and surfaced the resulting progress information through reporting.

sections.title: Reports and Charts
paragraphs: I built reporting views using Chart.js and react-chartjs-2.
The dashboard presented summary and detailed progress information through charts, reports, and drill-down views for teachers and administrators.

sections.title: Notifications
paragraphs: The dashboard included teacher notifications for important student activity and completion events.

sections.title: Favorite Programs
paragraphs: Teachers could mark commonly used programs as favorites to make frequently assigned curriculum easier to access.

sections.title: Class and Reward Settings
paragraphs: The dashboard exposed class-level configuration and reward settings used by the student applications.

sections.title: Mad Minute Integration
paragraphs: The React dashboard absorbed the specialized Mad Minute teacher controls into the main administration platform.
Teachers could configure Mad Minute behavior and access its specialized reporting without returning to the old standalone desktop dashboard.

sections.title: Read to Succeed Integration
paragraphs: Read to Succeed used a specialized student runtime but integrated into the same React administration and reporting platform.
Teachers managed its assignments, student progress, and reporting through the common dashboard.

sections.title: Spelling Editor Integration
paragraphs: The later web-based Spelling Editor had its own Angular application, but teachers launched and accessed it through the React Teacher Dashboard.
This kept specialized authoring tools connected to the main teacher workflow.

sections.title: Roster and SSO Integrations
paragraphs: The dashboard became the operational interface for multiple school rostering and authentication integrations.

sections.title: Long-Term Production Generation
paragraphs: The React dashboard was never replaced by another complete Teacher Dashboard generation.
It became the long-lived production administration and reporting system while additional features, integrations, and specialized tools continued to be added around it.

historicalNotes: The legacy portfolio card described this only as a React redesign of the Admin/Teacher Dashboard.
This was the 2019 React replacement for the earlier JavaScript Teacher Dashboard.
Jamie built the React application alone.
Jamie designed the UI/UX and reviewed the design with the owners for approval.
The backend remained primarily PHP + AWS SimpleDB / AWS while React became the frontend.
Redux, Redux-Observable, RxJS, and Axios were used for backend communication and asynchronous state orchestration.
Jamie found the conventional per-endpoint Redux/Redux-Observable structure too verbose, requiring roughly seven files per endpoint.
He consolidated request handling into one shared infrastructure path rather than creating the same Redux/RxJS boilerplate repeatedly.
Feature code supplied declarative request objects containing func, params, optional altName, and optional nextRequest.
nextRequest allowed asynchronous backend operations to be chained declaratively.
A recovered example chains getCustomer -> getAllPrograms -> getAllUserPrograms -> trackNewVersionTeacher -> getAllClasses -> getStudentsForClass -> getAllStudentsForSchool.
The request system should be described as a custom centralized pipeline built on top of Redux/RxJS rather than as replacing Redux entirely.
The dashboard supported teacher and administrator logins, with administrators able to access all teachers in their school.
This generation supported students belonging to multiple classes even without third-party roster integrations.

Major functionality included class/student management, assignments, pretests/posttests, reports/charts, notifications, favorites, class/reward settings, Mad Minute, Read to Succeed, Spelling Editor access, and school integrations.
Chart.js / react-chartjs-2 were used for charting.

The recovered package.json identifies React 16.8.6, Redux 4.0.1, Redux-Observable 1.1.0, RxJS 6.4.0, Axios 0.18.0, Bootstrap 4.3.1, Chart.js 2.8.0, React Router 5.0.0, Formik, Yup, Lodash, Ramda, Immer, and Styled Components.
The internal package/project name in the recovered package.json was arcshape2.
The React Teacher Dashboard was never replaced and remained the long-term production dashboard generation.
The broader history of Marks Manager and earlier Teacher Dashboard generations belongs in the separate Essential Skills Teacher Management & Reporting Systems umbrella card.
